sites.name: Launch Complex 39A
sites.siteName: Kennedy Space Center, Merritt Island, Florida
sites.mission: Apollo, Skylab, Space Shuttle, commercial crews
sites.categoryDetail: Heavy-lift launch pad — Saturn V, Shuttle, Falcon 9
sites.coordNote: Centre of pad 39A. The flame trench and hardstand are visible in satellite imagery.
sites.summary: The pad that sent humans to the Moon, then flew the Shuttle for 30 years, then became a commercial launch site.
narrative: Pad 39A was built for the Saturn V and first fired on 9 November 1967 with the uncrewed Apollo 4, an all-up test of the Moon rocket that engineers had decided to fly before putting a crew on it. Apollo 8 left from here on the first crewed flight around the Moon, Apollo 11 left from here on the first landing, and the pad went on to serve most of the lunar programme.

After Apollo, 39A was rebuilt for the Space Shuttle: the launch tower was replaced, the Saturn-era swing arms removed, and the pad's service structure redesigned around an orbiter standing vertically on an external tank. From 1981 to 2011 it launched Space Shuttle missions including the Hubble Space Telescope deployments and most of the assembly flights for the International Space Station.

Its third career began in 2014, when SpaceX leased the pad and modified it for Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy — including the return of Crew Dragon launches from American soil in 2020. Very little of the Apollo-era surface hardware survives; the concrete and the flame trench do. A pad is the one place where you can stand on the footprint of the Saturn V and watch a completely different rocket leave for orbit.

artifacts.name: Pad 39A hardstand and flame trench
artifacts.note: Saturn V-era concrete and the original crawlerway approach remain.

sites.name: Launch Complex 39B
sites.siteName: Kennedy Space Center, Merritt Island, Florida
sites.mission: Apollo 10, Skylab crews, Artemis
sites.categoryDetail: Heavy-lift launch pad — Saturn V, Shuttle, Space Launch System
sites.summary: The other Apollo Moon pad, later rebuilt for the Shuttle and then for the rocket that will return crews to the Moon.
narrative: Pad 39B flew the dress rehearsal for the first landing: Apollo 10, in May 1969, went to the Moon, separated its Lunar Module and descended to within 15 km of the surface before returning — everything except the landing itself. It then hosted three Skylab crews on Saturn IB rockets, using a smaller vehicle on a pad built for something much larger.

Like 39A it was converted for the Space Shuttle, and it carried missions that could not be flown from the other pad, including the 1986 return to flight. After the Shuttle retired, 39B was rebuilt again around the Space Launch System, with a new mobile launcher and a crew access arm.

On 16 November 2022 Artemis I lifted off from 39B, sending an uncrewed Orion capsule around the Moon and back. The pad that launched the dress rehearsal for Apollo 11 is now the pad for the programme intended to follow it.

facts.label: Current use
facts.value: NASA — Space Launch System and Artemis

sites.name: Launch Complex 34 — Apollo 1 memorial
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Apollo 1 (AS-204), Apollo 7
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — site of the Apollo 1 fire, later Apollo 7
sites.status: Decommissioned — concrete pad preserved as a memorial
sites.coordNote: Centre of the remaining pad 34 hardstand.
sites.summary: Where three astronauts died in a fire on the launch pad, and where the first Apollo crew later flew in their memory.
narrative: On 27 January 1967, during a plugs-out test of the Apollo 1 spacecraft at pad 34, a fire broke out in the pure-oxygen cabin. Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee died within seconds. The spacecraft had a hatch that could not be opened quickly against internal pressure, and the accident forced a complete redesign of the command module.

Pad 34 was rebuilt and, on 11 October 1968, launched Apollo 7 — the first crewed Apollo flight, and the mission that validated the redesigned spacecraft in Earth orbit. After Apollo 7 the pad was used for a few Saturn IB flights and then abandoned.

What remains is a concrete pedestal with the service structure legs cut off, standing in the Florida scrub. A plaque near the pad reads: In memory of those who made the ultimate sacrifice so others could reach for the stars. The launch complex is on the National Register of Historic Places; the gantry is gone, but the pad's four legs are still bolted to the concrete.

artifacts.name: Pad 34 concrete hardstand and service structure pedestal

facts.value: Virgil I. Grissom, Edward H. White II, Roger B. Chaffee

facts.value: Decommissioned; memorial on the National Register of Historic Places

sites.name: Launch Complex 19 — Gemini crewed launches
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Gemini 3 to Gemini 12
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — all ten crewed Gemini flights
sites.status: Decommissioned — pad and erector legs remain
sites.summary: The most reliably crewed pad in American history: ten launches, ten crews, no failures.
narrative: Between March 1965 and November 1966 every crewed Gemini mission left from pad 19 on a Titan II. The pad had a distinctive white erector that held the rocket horizontally, lifted it upright with the crew already aboard, and swung away at ignition. The two astronauts rode to the pad standing in the white room and then sat in the capsule while it was raised.

Gemini is where the techniques for Apollo were worked out: rendezvous and docking, spacewalks, multi-day flights, and the experience of flying a spacecraft rather than simply riding in it. All ten crewed flights launched successfully, a record no other pad in the world has matched for crewed vehicles.

The pad was deactivated in 1967 when Apollo moved to the much larger Saturn IB and Saturn V complexes. The hardstand and the twin rails of the erector are still visible among the scrub at Cape Canaveral.

sites.name: Launch Complex 14 — Mercury-Atlas
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Mercury-Atlas 6–9
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — orbital Mercury flights
sites.status: Decommissioned — pad preserved as a memorial
sites.summary: The pad from which John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth.
narrative: Complex 14 launched all four orbital Mercury missions. On 20 February 1962 Friendship 7 lifted off with John Glenn aboard and completed three orbits, restoring American confidence after the Soviet flights of Gagarin and Titov. Scott Carpenter, Wally Schirra and Gordon Cooper followed from the same pad.

Mercury-Atlas was a difficult combination: a converted intercontinental ballistic missile as a crew launcher, with the astronaut in a capsule barely big enough to sit in. Two of the four missions had significant malfunctions — Carpenter's fuel and attitude problems, Cooper's failure of the automatic control system, which he flew by hand.

The pad was deactivated in 1966. In 1997 a group of Mercury veterans restored part of the complex, and a memorial stands near the original blockhouse and the base of the red gantry that once held Friendship 7.

sites.name: Launch Complex 5 — Mercury-Redstone
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Mercury-Redstone 3 and 4
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — first American crewed spaceflights
sites.coordNote: Centre of launch complex 5, adjacent to pad 6.
sites.summary: The small concrete pad where Alan Shepard became the first American in space, seven weeks after Gagarin.
narrative: Complex 5 was built for the Redstone, a medium-range missile adapted to carry a Mercury capsule on a ballistic trajectory. On 5 May 1961 Freedom 7 lifted off with Alan Shepard aboard, flew 187 km downrange and splashed into the Atlantic 15 minutes later. It was not an orbit, but it was the flight that started American human spaceflight.

On 21 July 1961 Gus Grissom flew Liberty Bell 7 from the same pad. His capsule sank after splashdown when the hatch blew, and Grissom nearly drowned. He later commanded the first Gemini crewed flight and died in the Apollo 1 fire at pad 34, 4.5 km away along the same coastline.

The pad is preserved, with its blockhouse and the concrete ramp that carried the rocket to the launch mount. It is one of the few places where the physical scale of the first American space programme can be seen: the Redstone was 25 m tall, and the whole complex could fit inside the flame trench at pad 39A.

sites.name: Space Launch Complex 17 — the Mars pad
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Mars Polar Lander
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — most Mars surface missions of 1996–2008
sites.coordNote: Centres of pads 17A and 17B; the site was cleared in 2018.
sites.summary: One Delta II pad complex launched nearly every American spacecraft that landed on Mars between 1996 and 2008.
narrative: Pad 17A and its twin 17B opened in 1957 and spent most of their lives launching Delta rockets. Their most remarkable run came at the end of the Cold War: Mars Pathfinder left from 17A in December 1996, Mars Polar Lander from 17B in January 1999, and then both Mars Exploration Rovers in the summer of 2003 — Spirit from 17A, Opportunity from 17B, three weeks apart.

Phoenix left from 17A in August 2007, the last Mars mission to use the pad. The Delta II was retired soon afterwards, and the two towers were demolished in 2018; the concrete pads and their flame trenches remain.

The complex is a useful corrective to the idea that launch sites are monuments. Some of the most consequential pads in planetary exploration were built for a workhorse rocket, flew a handful of historic missions, and were then taken apart when the rocket went out of service.

facts.label: Mars launches
facts.value: Mars Pathfinder (1996), Mars Polar Lander (1999), Spirit (2003), Opportunity (2003), Phoenix (2007)

sites.name: Space Launch Complex 41
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Voyager 1 and 2, New Horizons, Mars 2020
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — outer planets and Mars 2020
sites.summary: Both Voyagers left from this pad, and so did the rover now caching samples on Mars.
narrative: Complex 41 was built for the Titan III-C and modified for the Titan IIIE/Centaur, the combination needed to throw heavy payloads onto escape trajectories. Voyager 2 launched from here on 20 August 1977; Voyager 1 followed on 5 September, on a faster trajectory that would carry it past Jupiter and Saturn and out of the solar system.

The pad was rebuilt in the 1990s for the Atlas V. From it left New Horizons to Pluto in 2006, the Juno orbiter to Jupiter in 2011, the OSIRIS-REx sample-return mission in 2016, and on 30 July 2020 the Mars 2020 mission carrying the Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter.
Voyager 1 and Perseverance, launched from the same concrete 43 years apart, are now the most distant human object and the most sophisticated machine on another planet. Both are still working.

sources.title: Cape Canaveral Space Launch Complex 41 coordinates

sites.name: Space Launch Complex 40
sites.siteName: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida
sites.mission: Falcon 9, Dragon, commercial resupply and crews
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — rebuilt commercial pad
sites.summary: A 1960s Titan pad that became the busiest commercial launch site in the world — after being destroyed and rebuilt.
narrative: Pad 40 opened in 1965 for Titan III launches and was used for military and planetary missions for four decades. SpaceX took it over in 2007 and flew its first Falcon 9 from it in June 2010.

On 1 September 2016 a Falcon 9 exploded during a static fire test, destroying the rocket, its AMOS-6 satellite payload and much of the pad. The company rebuilt the complex in less than a year and returned to flight from the same concrete in December 2017.

Since then 40 has launched cargo and crew Dragons, dozens of Starlink batches and planetary missions including the DART asteroid impactor. It is a rare example of a launch pad that has been both abandoned and revived — twice over, with the Titan and Falcon eras separated by a rebuild.

facts.label: 2016 accident
facts.value: Falcon 9 and AMOS-6 destroyed on the pad, 1 September 2016

sites.name: Vandenberg Space Launch Complex 3E
sites.mission: InSight, Mars Cube One
sites.categoryDetail: Launch pad — first interplanetary launch from the US West Coast
sites.coordNote: Pad centre, approximate to a few tens of metres.
sites.summary: InSight left Earth from California — the first planetary launch ever made from the west coast of the United States.
narrative: Almost every NASA planetary mission has launched from Florida, where the Atlantic provides a safe range for the drop stages. InSight broke that pattern. On 5 May 2018 an Atlas V lifted off from Vandenberg's pad 3E, flying south over the Pacific, because the mission's polar trajectory to Mars required a westward launch azimuth.

The rocket also carried Mars Cube One, two small CubeSats that flew separately to Mars and relayed InSight's entry, descent and landing telemetry back to Earth in real time — the first interplanetary CubeSats and the first time a Mars landing had been watched live by a dedicated relay.

The pad itself dates from 1962 and has launched Thor, Delta II and Atlas V rockets. It is a reminder that the geography of spaceflight is not fixed: a mission can require a launch site, a trajectory and a range that nobody had used for that purpose before.

facts.label: Payloads
facts.value: InSight lander and Mars Cube One (MarCO-A/B)

facts.label: Note
facts.value: First interplanetary launch from the US west coast

sites.name: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
sites.mission: Ranger, Surveyor, Voyager, Mars rovers, and many more
sites.program: NASA field centre (FFRDC managed by Caltech)
sites.categoryDetail: Laboratory and mission control
sites.summary: A graduate student project that turned into the place where America's robotic spacecraft are built and flown.
narrative: JPL began in 1936 with a group of Caltech students testing rocket motors in the Arroyo Seco. During the Second World War it became an Army facility; in 1958 it was transferred to the new civilian space agency, and it has managed NASA's planetary programmes ever since.

Every US spacecraft that has touched another world was largely designed, built or operated here: the Rangers that photographed the Moon before crashing into it, the Surveyors that landed, the Mariners, the Voyagers, the Vikings, the rovers from Sojourner to Perseverance. The laboratory also runs the Deep Space Network's operations, and its mission control rooms are the places where signals from spacecraft billions of kilometres away are received.

The campus is a working laboratory rather than a museum. Its buildings include the Space Flight Operations Facility, still in daily use; the nearby Arroyo Seco, where the first rockets were tested, is now a hiking trail with a small plaque.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 1936, by Caltech students; transferred to NASA in 1958

facts.label: Well-known missions
facts.value: Ranger, Surveyor, Voyager, Viking, Mars rovers, Cassini, Juno, Perseverance

facts.value: Robotic exploration of the solar system

sites.name: Johnson Space Center — Mission Control
sites.mission: Gemini, Apollo, Skylab, Space Shuttle, ISS
sites.categoryDetail: Crewed spaceflight centre and historic mission control room
sites.coordNote: Main campus centre point; the historic Mission Control room (Building 30) is on the south side.
sites.summary: The room where every Apollo landing was flown, and where the phrase Houston, we've had a problem was first heard.
narrative: The Manned Spacecraft Center opened in Houston in 1961, on land donated by Rice University, and was renamed for Lyndon Johnson in 1973. Its Flight Control Room 2 — now a National Historic Landmark — was the operational heart of the Apollo programme: the room where flight directors Gene Kranz, Chris Kraft and their teams made the decisions that determined whether a crew came home.

On 13 April 1970 Apollo 13's oxygen tank exploded while the spacecraft was 330,000 km from Earth. The room's response — powering down the command module, using the Lunar Module as a lifeboat, and improvising a carbon-dioxide scrubber from plastic bags and cardboard — is one of the more remarkable feats of engineering management in the 20th century.

Mission Control still operates the International Space Station from the same building complex. The historic room has been restored to its Apollo-era appearance, down to the consoles, the flight director's loop and the ashtrays. Tours of Johnson Space Center include the room, and it is one of the few places where the physical workplace of space exploration has been preserved.

facts.label: Apollo 13
facts.value: Rescue coordinated from Flight Control Room 2, April 1970

facts.label: Current role
facts.value: ISS operations, astronaut training, Orion programme

sites.name: Vehicle Assembly Building
sites.mission: Saturn V, Space Shuttle, Space Launch System
sites.categoryDetail: Vertical assembly building
sites.summary: One of the largest buildings in the world, built to stack Moon rockets indoors and still used to assemble rockets today.
narrative: The Vehicle Assembly Building is 160 m tall, 218 m long and encloses 3.7 million cubic metres — large enough that it has its own weather, and that the American flag painted on its side is 64 m wide. It was built so that a complete Saturn V could be stacked vertically indoors, out of the Florida rain, before being carried to the pad on a crawler.

Four high bays held the Apollo rockets; the same building was later converted for the Space Shuttle, with platforms and a lifting frame built around the orbiter and its external tank. After the Shuttle era it was modified again for the Space Launch System, whose core stage and boosters were assembled in the same high bay.

Its most distinctive feature is practical: the huge doors take 45 minutes to open, and the building's air conditioning is sized to keep the interior from condensing on a rocket's cryogenic tanks. The VAB is still the place where American heavy-lift rockets are put together, and it is visible from most of the Space Coast.

sites.name: Marshall Space Flight Center
sites.mission: Saturn V, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Hubble Space Telescope
sites.categoryDetail: Propulsion and payload development centre
sites.summary: The centre that developed the Saturn V, built the lunar rover, and later managed the Hubble Space Telescope.
narrative: Marshall Space Flight Center was established in 1960 around Wernher von Braun's rocket team, which had been developing ballistic missiles for the US Army at Redstone Arsenal. Its first great project was the Saturn family: the Saturn I, Saturn IB and Saturn V launch vehicles, developed and tested mostly in Huntsville and at the Mississippi Test Facility downriver.

After Apollo, Marshall built the Lunar Roving Vehicle — a contract that produced three flight vehicles and changed what crews could do on the surface. The centre also developed the Shuttle's solid rocket boosters and external tank, managed the Hubble Space Telescope, and now leads the Space Launch System.

The centre's test stands and the Saturn V display at the adjacent US Space & Rocket Center make it one of the few places where the full scale of the Moon rocket can be seen at ground level — a complete Saturn V lying on its side in a hall built around it.

facts.label: Key projects
facts.value: Saturn I/IB/V, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Shuttle boosters, Hubble, SLS

sites.name: Michoud Assembly Facility
sites.mission: Saturn V first stages, Shuttle external tanks, SLS core stage
sites.categoryDetail: Large-scale manufacturing plant
sites.summary: Where the first stage of every Saturn V was welded together, and where Shuttle tanks and SLS core stages were built.
narrative: Michoud is a former war-time shipyard east of New Orleans with some of the largest manufacturing buildings in the world. NASA took it over in 1961 to build the Saturn V's first stage, the S-IC: 42 m long, 10 m in diameter, with five F-1 engines and a thrust of 34 meganewtons.

Thirteen S-IC stages were built and flown. After Apollo the plant switched to the Space Shuttle external tank, producing 136 of them, and then to the core stage of the Space Launch System. In 2018 the plant was in the path of Hurricane Katrina's successors and has been rebuilt several times; the tooling, cranes and vertical assembly cells are still in use.

Michoud is the kind of place that never appears in a launch highlight reel, but every Saturn V that went to the Moon began here, as sheets of aluminium alloy welded in a building long enough to hide a rocket inside.

sites.name: Stennis Space Center test stands
sites.mission: Saturn V stage testing, Shuttle main engine testing, SLS
sites.categoryDetail: Rocket propulsion test facility
sites.coordNote: Facility centre point; individual test stands are within a few kilometres.
sites.summary: The stand where every Saturn V first stage was fired before it was allowed near a launch pad.
narrative: Stennis, originally the Mississippi Test Facility, was built in the 1960s on a large tract of swamp and pine forest north of New Orleans. Its test stands were designed for the acoustic and physical violence of firing a Saturn V first stage on the ground: the B-1 and B-2 stands can hold a complete S-IC stage while all five F-1 engines run.

Every flight Saturn V first stage was acceptance-tested here, as were the second stages. After Apollo the site tested Space Shuttle main engines — more than two million seconds of firing over three decades — and now tests the core stage of the Space Launch System.

The test stands are surrounded by a buffer of more than 50,000 hectares, which has become a wildlife refuge. Alligators and bald eagles live inside the perimeter of a facility built to make the loudest machines in the world.

facts.label: Saturn V testing
facts.value: All flight S-IC first stages acceptance-fired

sites.name: Ames Research Center
sites.mission: LCROSS, Kepler, Pioneer, lunar mission support
sites.categoryDetail: Research centre — lunar and planetary science
sites.summary: A wind-tunnel laboratory that became the home of NASA's lunar impactor and the search for other Earths.
narrative: Ames was founded in 1939 as an aeronautical laboratory and grew into a centre for space science, supercomputing and astrobiology. Its wind tunnels tested the shapes of Mercury capsules and the Space Shuttle; its life scientists ran the experiments that asked whether biology could survive on other worlds.

Ames managed the LCROSS mission, which fired a Centaur stage into Cabeus crater in 2009 and found water in the plume. It also ran the Kepler space telescope, which discovered thousands of exoplanets, and the Lunar Prospector mission that first detected hydrogen at the lunar poles.

The centre sits beside Moffett Field, whose enormous Hangar One — built for airships in the 1930s — is one of the most recognisable structures in the Bay Area. The campus still works on lunar science, planetary protection and the design of instruments for future landers.

sites.name: Goddard Space Flight Center
sites.mission: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, NSSDCA, Explorer missions
sites.categoryDetail: Space science centre and national data archive
sites.summary: Home of the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and of the archive this archive depends on.
narrative: Goddard was NASA's first space flight centre, established in 1959, and it has managed an extraordinary fraction of the agency's scientific spacecraft. It runs the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, whose cameras produced the coordinates used throughout this archive, and it hosts the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDCA) and the Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, where mission records, images and instrument data are preserved.

The centre also built and operates the networks that talk to spacecraft: the Near Earth Network and the Space Network are coordinated from Greenbelt, and the Deep Space Network's operations are shared with JPL.

The NSSDCA pages documenting lunar landing sites and anthropogenic impacts were written and maintained here by Dr. David R. Williams. Without that catalogue, an archive of abandoned spacecraft would have to start from scratch; with it, every marker on the Moon in this application can be traced to a specific table with a specific author.

facts.label: Key missions
facts.value: LRO, Hubble operations, Explorers, JWST operations

facts.label: Data archive
facts.value: NSSDCA and the Space Science Data Coordinated Archive

sites.name: White Sands Missile Range
sites.mission: V-2 tests, Space Shuttle landing site, Apollo-era testing
sites.categoryDetail: Test range and emergency Shuttle landing site
sites.coordNote: Range headquarters area; the historic launch complexes are spread across the range.
sites.summary: Where captured V-2s were fired into the desert, and where one Space Shuttle landed on a gypsum flat.
narrative: In 1946 captured German V-2 rockets were assembled and fired from White Sands, carrying instruments to the edge of space. Those flights produced the first photographs of Earth from high altitude and some of the earliest data on the upper atmosphere, and they established the practice of launching scientific payloads on military rockets.

The range's most unusual spaceflight connection is a landing: on 30 March 1982 Space Shuttle Columbia touched down on Northrup Strip at White Sands, the only Shuttle landing in the continental United States outside Florida. The site had been prepared as a backup runway, and high winds in Florida forced its only operational use; the gypsum dust that coated the orbiter caused problems for weeks afterwards.

The range is still active, and the Trinity Site, where the first nuclear device was tested in 1945, lies within its boundary. Its landscape of white dunes and black lava is used to this day for testing instruments that will operate on other planets.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: New Mexico, between Las Cruces and Alamogordo

sites.name: Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex
sites.mission: Apollo tracking, Voyager, Mars missions
sites.categoryDetail: Deep Space Network antenna complex
sites.coordNote: Complex centre point; individual antennas are within a few kilometres.
sites.summary: A cluster of dishes in the Mojave that has been listening to spacecraft since the first American lunar probes.
narrative: Goldstone began as a single 26 m antenna in 1958, built to track the Pioneer lunar probes. It grew into one of the three complexes of NASA's Deep Space Network, alongside Madrid and Canberra, positioned roughly 120° apart so that at least one can see any spacecraft at any time.

The 70 m DSS-14 antenna, completed in 1966, was built for the Apollo programme and later upgraded. It is the largest fully steerable antenna in the network and has tracked Voyager 1 and 2 into interstellar space, received data from every Mars surface mission, and performed radar observations of near-Earth asteroids.

The complex is in the desert for a reason: radio quiet. Its dishes are now surrounded by the Mojave National Preserve, and the site operates a visitor centre with one of the antennas — a 34 m dish — open for tours.

facts.value: Deep Space Network — communications and tracking

sites.name: Parkes Observatory — the dish that carried Apollo 11
sites.mission: Apollo 11 television relay, planetary radar
sites.categoryDetail: Radio telescope used for NASA mission support
sites.coordNote: Centre of the 64 m dish at the Parkes Observatory.
sites.summary: The Australian dish that received most of the world's television pictures of the first Moon landing.
narrative: Parkes is a 64 m radio telescope in the sheep country of New South Wales, built in 1961. When Apollo 11 flew, NASA needed a large antenna in the southern hemisphere to receive the television signal from the lunar surface during the long Australian night, and Parkes was the biggest and best available.

On 21 July 1969 the dish caught the signal from the Lunar Module's camera and passed it to the tracking station network for distribution. The moment Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon was received by the smaller antenna at Honeysuckle Creek near Canberra, which had a better angle; a few minutes later the feed switched to Parkes, which carried most of the rest of the broadcast. The images the world remembers — the ghostly, high-contrast picture of a man on the Moon — came through these antennas.

Parkes is still a working observatory, used for pulsar timing, fast radio bursts and spacecraft tracking. The story of that night was made into the film The Dish, which is more accurate about the sheep than about the timing.

facts.label: Apollo 11 role
facts.value: Received and relayed most of the lunar surface television, 21 July 1969

facts.label: Still operating
facts.value: Yes — pulsars, fast radio bursts, spacecraft tracking

sites.name: Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station
sites.siteName: Namadgi National Park, Australian Capital Territory
sites.mission: Apollo 11 first television, Apollo tracking
sites.categoryDetail: Tracking station — received the first steps on the Moon
sites.coordNote: Site of the former station; the 26 m antenna was moved to Tidbinbilla in 1983.
sites.summary: A 26 m dish in the hills above Canberra that received the first human footsteps on the Moon.
narrative: Honeysuckle Creek was one of NASA's Manned Space Flight Network stations, built in the bush south of Canberra to support crewed missions in the southern hemisphere. On 21 July 1969 its 26 m antenna was pointed at the Moon as Armstrong came down the ladder, and it received the first television pictures — inverted and high-contrast, but recognisably a man.

After about eight minutes the feed was switched to the larger Parkes dish, which had a better view and signal. Honeysuckle Creek continued to support Apollo and later missions, including the Apollo-Soyuz flight, and closed in 1981. Its antenna was moved to the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex at Tidbinbilla, where it was used for another two decades.

The site is now a grassy clearing in Namadgi National Park with a few concrete footings and a plaque — one of the quietest places in the history of space exploration, and one of the most consequential.

facts.label: Apollo 11 first TV
facts.value: Received the first lunar surface images, 21 July 1969

facts.label: Current status
facts.value: Footings and plaque in Namadgi National Park

sites.name: Langley Research Center
sites.mission: Viking project management, Lunar Orbiter, Mercury
sites.categoryDetail: Research centre — early human spaceflight and Mars landers
sites.summary: America's oldest aeronautics laboratory, which managed the Viking landers and tested the Mercury capsule.
narrative: Langley was established in 1917 as an aeronautical laboratory and became the birthplace of American human spaceflight: the Mercury capsule was designed and tested here, and the original seven astronauts trained partly in its facilities. Its engineers ran the wind tunnel and flight tests that decided what a spacecraft should look like.

Langley also managed the Lunar Orbiter programme, which photographed 99% of the Moon and produced the maps Apollo used, and the Viking project, which put two landers on Mars in 1976 — the first successful landing on another planet. Viking's biology experiments and its images of a rust-coloured plain transformed the public idea of Mars.

The centre is still active in aeronautics, atmospheric science and planetary instrument development. Its headquarters building dates from the 1920s, and the centre's wind tunnels include some of the oldest large-scale facilities in the world still in use.
